column15: According to the NSW Government website (current as of 4 August 2020 and last updated as of 23 July  2020) all students were expected to attend classes on campus unless they were unwell or had a medical certificate to justify their absence. Students were not expected to follow 1.5m social distancing guidelines. However, there were some COVID-safe restrictions in place.    Staff and students who had been to Victoria in the past 14 days and did not live in a border town were required to self-isolate. Students who had been to Victoria in the past 14 days and were returning to boarding schools were also required to obtain a negative COVID-19 test on day 10 of isolation before returning to school.  Good hygiene practices were promoted in schools, and all visitors were required to adhere to safety protocols. Non-essential adults were prohibited from attending school events or schools grounds unless they had obtained permission from school principals. Schools received extra supplies of cleaning products, as well as additional cleaning of high-touch areas. Large arts and sports events were cancelled or delayed until further notice, and international excursions were cancelled. School camps, excursions, and large events involving parents were put on hold.    This was a continuation of existing restrictions. column15: A continuation of existing policies. Schools are not required to mandate masks or conduct temperature checks. Target areas include high-touch areas and other hard surfaces, door handles, lockers, light switches and handrails in stairways and movement areas. column24: As published by the NSW Government, a number of workplace restrictions were in place from 28 September 2020. Minister for Health and Medical Research Brad Hazzard has directed that all employers must allow employees to work at home if it is reasonably practicable to do so, a policy action similar to a recommendation. Workplaces providing direct services to members of the public are allowed to open, but must develop and comply with a COVID-19 Safety Plan and enforce density limits of 4 square metres per person.     This represents a continuation of existing policy, and is implemented without any regional variation.     http://web.archive.org/web/20220222100234/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20%28COVID-19%20Restrictions%20on%20Gathering%20and%20Movement%29%20Order%20%28No%205%29%202020_201123.pdf
column33: As published by the NSW Government, a number of restrictions on large public events are in place. All public events must develop a COVID-19 safety plan and maintain a density of 1 person per 4 square meters, with a maximum attendance cap placed depending on type of events. The maximum attendance cap extends to 10,000 persons at major recreational sporting facilities, where attendance is ticketed and this number does not represent more than 25% of maximum capacity.    This is a continuation of existing policy, and implemented without any regional variation.    https://web.archive.org/web/20201203013015/https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20(COVID-19%20Restrictions%20on%20Gathering%20and%20Movement)%20Order%20(No%205)%202020_201023.pdf  https://web.archive.org/web/20201123035056/https://www.nsw.gov.au/covid-19/what-you-can-and-cant-do-under-rules
column42: As published by the NSW Government, gatherings in residential premises are limited to include a maximum of 20 visitors. column42: As announced by Premier Gladys Berejiklian on 23/12/2020, restrictions on gatherings in the Northern Beaches and the Greater Sydney Area are being modified and extended until 26/12/2020.    In the northern zone of the Northern Beaches, residents are able to visit the homes of others in this area, with a maximum of 5 visitors including Children.    In the southern zone of the Northern Beaches, residents are allowed to up to 10 visitors in their home, plus primary school aged children and younger. These visitors must not come from the northern zone, but can include residents of either the southern zone or the rest of Greater Sydney.    In the Greater Sydney region,  the restriction on household gatherings to 10 visitor remains, but primary school-aged children and younger are no longer counted in this cap.     This small loosening in restrictions intends to balance the social desire of contact during the Christmas period and concerns about community transmission.    In other areas of the state, previous restrictions remain in place. column33: The COVID-19 Directions (No. 14) 2020 Directions for Gatherings were in place between midnight on 30 March 2020 and midnight on 20 April 2020.    According to these directions, a maximum of 10 people were allowed to gather together in an undivided area outdoors. A maximum of 10 people were allowed to gather together in an undivided space indoors. Indoor gatherings were required to follow a one person per four square metre rule.    The following activities were exempt from these restrictions:  	- Gatherings on residential premises  	- Gatherings for the purposes of conducting emergency services  	- Gatherings inside private motor vehicles or commercial transport  	- Gatherings at places of transit such as stations  	- Gathering for the purposes of maintaining normal activities at workplaces (such as correctional facilities, educational facilities, permitted retail, accommodation services, healthcare services, offices and other workplaces)    In addition to these directions, the COVID-19 Directions (No. 18) 2020 Directions to Close Public Places, Services and Activities, which were in place between 11:59pm on 9 April 2020 and 11:59pm on 15 April 2020, prohibited the following businesses and activities from operating:    - Restaurants and food courts  - Casinos and businesses with totalisators and gaming machine licenses  - Entertainment and amusement venues  - Indoor markets (other than food markets)  - Places that provide beauty therapy, body art, and wellnesses services  - Strip clubs and other businesses which provide sexual services  - Pools, parks, recreation centres, and premises which provide physical training indoors  - Businesses that provide physical training indoors, as well as those that provide physical training indoors with more than 2 people from different households  - Public institutions, places of interest, and places of worship    The directions in place between 7-13 April 2020 were a continuation of existing policy. column77: According to the Treasury, the JobKeeper Payment became available introduced from 30 March 2020 until 27 September 2020.    The JobKeeper Payment is a payment made to eligible businesses and not-for-profits affected by the Coronavirus to support them in retaining employees. Businesses must have paid their employees before they are entitled to receive the JobKeeper payment.     Where an employee’s total remuneration is less than $1,500 per fortnight (before tax), or has been stood down, the employer must provide the employee at least $1,500 per fortnight (before tax). Where an employee earns more than $1,500 per fortnight, employers can use the payment to subsidise the employee’s wages.    Self-employed individuals will also be eligible to receive the JobKeeper payment. Self-employed individuals are not informal workers as they operate their own business with an ABN in order to be eligible to the JobKeeper Payment. Therefore, this scheme was available to formal workers.    This represents a 2F level of policy as of 27 April 2020 in Australia.    Archived link:  https://web.archive.org/web/20220304125206/https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-04/JobKeeper_frequently_asked_questions_2.pdf

column115: According to NT government announcement:  To protect older Australians and those with compromised immune systems, we all need to work together to help stop the spread of coronavirus (COVID-19).    We also need to be particularly sensitive with people living with dementia or where there is a limited capacity to communicate verbally or express pain and discomfort.    Their ability to follow instruction or to alert others about potential symptoms may be challenging. In this situation, observation by someone who knows the person may assist in identifying changes in their health.    If you have returned from overseas or been in contact with someone confirmed to have coronavirus (COVID-19) in the last 14 days, you will not be able to visit a residential aged care facility.    You are also not allowed to visit if you have a fever, symptoms of a respiratory illness, or if you have not been vaccinated against influenza.    From 1 May 2020, you must have your influenza vaccination in order to visit an aged care facility.    Visits should be short, and conducted in the resident’s room, outside, or in a specific designated area (not a communal space).    Each resident may have no more than two visitors, including doctors, at a time.    Visits by children aged 16 years and under are not permitted except in special circumstances.    You and anyone else who is visiting will need to wash your hands before entering and leaving a resident’s room. column74: International Travel Restrictions    The National Cabinet noted the AHPPC’s advice on high-risk countries for COVID-19 importation risk and its continued support for the 14 day self isolation requirement for all returning travellers. column77: Continuation of policy from Mar 22, 2020 where the Australian Government announced a second economic support package, bringing additional support of around $66 billion. column115: People must not enter aged care facilities unless they:  -	work at the facility  -	are providing goods or services necessary for the facility's operation  -	are providing healthcare or medicine to a resident  -	are providing care and support to a resident, for up to 2 hours per day  -	are there for emergency or law enforcement purposes  -	are a prospective resident at the facility  -	are providing legal services to a resident  -	are performing regulatory functions (e.g. an inspection of the facility). column69: There is no longer any requirement to quarantine for 14 days before entering a remote community in NT. Residents can move freely between their communities, homelands, country and town. column115: In addition to practising good hygiene and physical distancing, there will be restrictions on visits to residential aged care facilities.   -	Large group visits, gatherings and external excursions are postponed. column77: The JobKeeper Wage Subsidy was in place throughout June 2020. This subsidy payment gave eligible workers $1500 per fortnight. column15: This is a continuation of the existing policy that took effect since the beginning of term 3 with no regional variation.     Education is now compulsory in the Northern Territory, and all children of compulsory school age are required to physically attend school. However, students who are unwell must remain at home and parents/carers should notify the school. The school will provide the student with learning from home materials to ensure that they can continue to learn during this period.   Some measures remain in place to minimize the risk of the spread of the virus, including enhanced hygiene practices, and restriction on accessing school grounds for people including staff who are either feeling unwell, awaiting covid-19 test outcome, have travelled to hotspot areas or have been directed to quarantine/self-isolate. All schools in the Northern Territory have received additional funding to enable them to increase their current cleaning regime.  Given that physical attendance is now compulsory and there is no mention of requirements to isolate if a class member tests positive, the situation is coded at a zero level.     https://web.archive.org/web/20200803155034/https://education.nt.gov.au/publications/information-for-term-3-2020
column24: This is a continuation of the existing policy that has been in place since early June as NT moved into the final stage of the reopening roadmap. No regional variation. column33: This is a continuation of the existing policy that have been in place since early June when NT moved into the final stage of the three-stage roadmap. No regional variation. column42: This is a continuation of the existing policy that have been in place since early June when NT moved into the final stage of the three-stage roadmap. No regional variation.  There are different requirements in place for gathering depending on the size of your event:  •	Events with less than 100 people do not require completion of a checklist or safety plan, however the physical distancing and hygiene principles should still be considered and implemented.  •	Events and public gatherings of 100 to 500 people must complete a covid-19 safety checklist to demonstrate commitment to the key principles.  •	Major events and public gatherings of over 500 people must submit a Covid-19 Event Safety Plan and receive formal approval from the Chief Health Officer prior to the event proceeding.    https://web.archive.org/web/20200806173124/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/roadmap-new-normal/business/guidelines-for-events-and-gatherings#/more_than_500_people
column51: This is a continuation of the existing policy with no regional variation. To minimise the risk of contracting or spreading coronavirus (COVID-19), passengers must practice good hygiene, physical distancing where possible, and sitting in the back seat of vehicles when using ridesharing or taxi services. Non-essential travel is still to be avoided. column60: As NT moved into the final stage of the three-stage roadmap in early June (continuation of the current policy), all businesses and organisations are allowed to operate, provided that they meet the requirements around the principles of physical distancing and hygiene practice. column115: According to the Covid-19 Direction (No. 40) 2020 Direction for Aged Care Facilities signed on 24 June (a continuation of the existing policy), visitors to residential aged care are allowed but under strict conditions that is as follow:  •	Each visit to a resident of the facility is limited to one individual visitor at a time or, if 2 persons are visiting a resident together, those 2 persons. -   •	Physical distancing practice where possible is encouraged. column115: According to NT government announcement:  A person must not enter or remain on the premises:  •	if they have symptoms which may be consistent with coronavirus (COVID-19)  •	if they have not had their flu vaccine  •	are under the age of 16 where they are not providing end of life support to a resident  •	have been in contact with a person with coronavirus (COVID-19).  A person must not enter or remain on the premises of an aged care facility unless the person is one of the following:  •	an officer, employee or contractor of the facility  •	a person providing goods or services necessary for the operation of the facility  •	a person providing health, medical or pharmaceutical goods or services to a resident of the facility  •	a person providing end of life support to a resident of the facility  •	a person required for emergency management or law enforcement  •	a prospective resident of the facility  •	a legal practitioner providing legal services to a resident of the facility  o	A legal practitioner entering the premises of the facility:  ?	(a) to take instructions from a client who is a resident of the facility or  ?	(b) for the purpose of executing a will by a client who is a resident of the facility.  •	a person performing regulatory functions or duties in relation to the facility, including an inspection of the facility.  •	Visitors  •	If you have returned from overseas or been in contact with someone confirmed to have coronavirus (COVID-19) in the last 14 days, you will not be able to visit a residential aged care facility.  •	You are also not allowed to visit if you have a fever, symptoms of a respiratory illness, or if you have not been vaccinated against influenza.  •	From 1 May 2020, you must have your influenza vaccination in order to visit an aged care facility.  •	Visits should be short, and conducted in the resident’s room, outside, or in a specific designated area (not a communal space).  •	Each resident may have no more than two visitors, including doctors, at a time.  •	Visits by children aged 16 years and under are not permitted except in special circumstances.  •	You and anyone else who is visiting will need to wash your hands before entering and leaving a resident’s room.  •	You will also be encouraged to practise physical distancing where possible, including to stay away when unwell. column88: According to Interim infection prevention and control guidelines for the management of COVID-19 in healthcare settings published by Queensland Health (Version 1.8; 19 February 2020), it states that patients who meet the suspected case definition should have laboratory testing performed.  The meaning of suspect is referred to Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19): CDNA National guidelines for public health units. It also suggests that patients meeting the suspect case definition should be tested for SARS-CoV-2.    According to the definition (see note), it appears that only people who meet certain criteria can get tested, such as showing COVID-19 symptoms, being a close contact, etc.    Additionally, according to Coronavirus (COVID-19) update for GPs published by the Queensland Government on 17 March 2020, it states that GPs can request a COVID-19 test at no out-of-pocket cost to the patient if the requesting medical practitioner suspects their patient is at risk of having COVID-19.     This represents a level 2 restriction in Queensland.    Note:  The definition of ‘suspect case’:  A. If the patient satisfies epidemiological and clinical criteria, they are classified as a suspect case.    Epidemiological criteria  -	International travel in the 14 days before illness onset.  OR  -	Close contact (see Contact definition below) in 14 days before illness onset with a confirmed case of COVID-19.    Clinical criteria  -	Fever.  OR  -	Acute respiratory infection (e.g. shortness of breath, cough, sore throat) with or  without fever.    B. If the patient has severe bilateral community-acquired pneumonia (critically ill*) and no other cause is identified, with or without recent international travel, they are classified as a suspect case.    *requiring care in ICU/HDU, or for patients in which ICU care is not appropriate, respiratory or multiorgan failure. Clinical judgement should be exercised considering the likelihood of COVID-19.    C. If any healthcare worker with direct patient contact has a fever (=37.5) AND an acute respiratory infection (e.g. shortness of breath, cough, sore throat), they are classified as a suspect case (see Healthcare workers for further information).    Archived link:  https://web.archive.org/web/20200301185545/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0038/939656/qh-covid-19-Infection-control-guidelines.pdf    https://web.archive.org/web/20200319221006/https://www1.health.gov.au/internet/main/publishing.nsf/Content/cdna-song-novel-coronavirus.htm    https://web.archive.org/web/20220421021843/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0035/947654/covid-19-update-GPs.pdf    https://web.archive.org/web/20200314100001/https://www1.health.gov.au/internet/main/publishing.nsf/Content/7A8654A8CB144F5FCA2584F8001F91E2/$File/interim-COVID-19-SoNG-v2.0.pdf
column90: According to the Queensland Government’s coronavirus update published on 10 March 2020 and a website of it updated on 13 March 2020, it suggests that Queensland’s contact tracing methods are tried and tested. Only those who have had face-to-face contact with a confirmed case for a period over 15 minutes, or those who have shared an enclosed space with a confirmed case for a prolonged period of more than two hours, are considered as a close contact.    The website also states contact tracing procedures:  -	As soon as an individual returns a positive result for COVID-19, just like with other contagious viruses such as measles, we undertake what is called contact tracing to prevent the infection spreading further through the community.    -	As part of this process, we speak to the patient to identify anyone who might have had close contact with them during their infectious window.    -	If there are people who are considered as close contacts, who are at a higher risk, our staff follow up with them directly.  If they begin showing symptoms, we assess them faster and take the right action.    If we can’t identify people who could have been in close contact with a confirmed case, we will issue a public health alert with specific dates, times and locations that the public should be aware of. Only people who match the exact criteria provided need to contact us.    Additionally, according to the Queensland Government’s coronavirus update published on 16 March 2020, it suggests Queensland Health is conducting contact tracing of new cases, and it will notify the community if any other public health alerts are required.    This represents the Queensland Government is implementing comprehensive contact tracing as of 16 March 2020. column115: As of 21 March 2020, the Aged Care Direction becomes effective. The Direction is to restrict contact between residents and non-residents of a residential aged care facility and direct measures that aged care facilities must put in place for visitors to the facility.    The Direction prohibits people from entering or remaining on the premises of a residential aged care facility in Queensland. Certain groups of people are exempted from the prohibition, such as employees or contractors in the facilities, people visiting the residential aged care facility for the purposes of end of life support for a resident of the facility, people visiting the residential aged care facility to provide goods or services, etc. Those exempted groups are also subject to other requirements such as having a temperature equal to or higher than 37.5 degrees or symptoms of acute respiratory infection, being under 16 years (unless the visit is for the purposes of end of life support for a resident), etc.    It also states that the operator of a residential aged care facility in Queensland must not permit a resident, excluding an end of life resident, to leave the facility except to receive or access health care or in the case of emergency.     Since the Direction largely prohibits external visitors from entering or remaining on the premises of a residential aged care facility in Queensland, and more importantly, it restricts the residents’ movement with minimal exceptions, it is more likely to be considered as a level 3G of restriction.    This represents a stringent policy of significant changes to pre-covid times as of 21 March 2020 in Queensland. column88: People who have fever or respiratory symptoms and who have been overseas in the past 14 days, or are a close contact of a confirmed COVID-19 case, should get tested. People who work in high-risk settings; who live in Brisbane, the Gold Coast or Cairns; who have been in another state or to a COVID-19 hotspot; or live in a First Nations community may also get tested if they develop symptoms. See https://web.archive.org/web/20200414014418/https://www.qld.gov.au/health/conditions/health-alerts/coronavirus-covid-19/take-action/testing-and-fever-clinics.
column90: Since at least March 23, 2020, the Queensland Government conducts comprehensive manual contact tracing for all confirmed COVID-19 cases. See https://web.archive.org/web/20200409113416/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/news-events/news/contact-tracing-novel-coronavirus-covid-19-confirmed-case-notify-Queensland.
column103: As of April 14, 2020, the Queensland Government does not specifically recommend that people wear face masks, unless they are unwell or have recently travelled overseas. See https://web.archive.org/web/20200414014100/https://www.qld.gov.au/health/conditions/health-alerts/coronavirus-covid-19/take-action/coronavirus-prevention.
column115: Since 21 March 2020, non-residents have been prohibited from entering aged care facilities unless they:   - work at the facility;   - are providing essential goods or services;   - are providing medical care to residents;   - are visiting to provide care or support;   - are present for emergency management or law enforcement;   - or are a prospective resident.     People within these permitted categories must still not enter if they:  - have been overseas in the past 14 days;   - have been in contact with a COVID-19 case in the past 14 days;   - they have respiratory symptoms, or a fever of 37.5° or higher;   - they are not vaccinated against influenza;   - or they are under 16 years of age.  See https://web.archive.org/web/20200813100209/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/revoked/aged-care-1.

column24: Under public health directions in force since 9 April 2020 (see http://web.archive.org/web/20220320031721/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/revoked/non-essential-business-closure-direction-4), most businesses deemed "non-essential" must close. These include retail food services such as cafes, restaurants and food courts (except for takeaway and delivery), auction houses, weapons dealers, beauty and personal care services, entertainment venues, leisure and recreation venues, accommodation facilities, museums, libraries, and community centres. Weddings and funerals may host up to 5 and 10 people, respectively. This is essentially a continuation of the previous rules, because changes from the previous directions (in place from 31 March–8 April 2020) are minimal.

column69: As of April 10, 2020, all travellers from other states and territories must self-isolate for 14 days, unless exempt. Exempt travellers include Queensland residents, travellers transiting through an airport to go to another state, government officials, health practitioners, emergency service workers, transport and freight workers, people with certain specialist skills, people living and working near the border with other states, and people entering Queensland for compassionate reasons. Exempt people must still self-isolate if they have been to "particular areas of Australia" (presumably COVID-19 hotspots) or if they have been overseas in the previous 14 days.   This is largely a continuation of the previous restrictions, with the only changes being that people moving to Queensland permanently must self-isolate for 14 days upon entry, and that people transiting through airports are specifically designated as exempt. See http://web.archive.org/web/20211006074440/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/revoked/border-restrictions-3.

column77: As of 13 April 2020, there continues to be some income support provided to formal workers in Australia. This continues from 11 April 2020, when the Australian Government last updated its JobKeeper scheme, where workers are given 1500AUD per fortnight (750AUD per week) (link 1). The median weekly income in Australia during 2020 was 1150AUD (link 2), so the government is replacing >50% of lost income.   Archived weblinks:  1. https://web.archive.org/web/20200421143110/https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-04/JobKeeper_frequently_asked_questions_2.pdf  2. https://web.archive.org/web/20220326022903/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-working-conditions/employee-earnings/latest-release

column15: Between the 15th and the 19th of April, Queensland students were on school holidays (which started early due to Covid-19. It was also announced by the Queensland Government that schools and community kindergartens would move to a home-based learning model from the 20th of April (start of Term 2) until at least the 22nd of May. Children of essential workers or those who were considered vulnerable were allowed to attend school if they were unable to remain at home.   https://web.archive.org/web/20200414134031/https://qed.qld.gov.au/about-us/news-and-media/novel-coronavirus
column24: Many non-essential businesses and activities were closed or heavily restricted between the 15th and the 21st of April. Notably, retail food services were limited to takeaway and delivery only, hairdressers and barbers remained open provided businesses followed density requirements, entertainment venues, retail and most non-residential institutions remained closed. A full list of business restrictions and closures was made available on the Queensland Health website.  These restrictions represent a continuation of the existing policy.  https://web.archive.org/web/20200422022924/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/non-essential-business-closure-direction

column51: Between the 15th and the 21st of April, all timetabled public transport services continued to run as scheduled with additional cleaning on public transport vehicles. However, the Queensland Governments advice was to limit all non-essential travel, travel outside of peak times where possible, practice good hand and respiratory hygiene and to stay home if unwell.  https://web.archive.org/web/20200414133238/https://translink.com.au/service-updates/274176
column60: From the 2nd of April, Queensland was under stay at home restrictions and were required to not leave their principle place of residence except for permitted purposes. Those included;  •	to obtain food or other essential goods or services;  •	to obtain medical treatment or other health care services;  •	to engage in physical exercise;  •	to perform work or volunteering, or carry out or conduct an essential business, activity or undertaking, and the work, business activity or undertaking to be performed is of a nature that cannot reasonably be performed from the person’s principal place of residence;  •	to visit another person’s residence (as one of no more than two visitors)  •	education and early childhood workers may travel to and from their home centre over the term 1 break;  •	to visit a terminally ill relative or to attend a funeral or wedding, subject to any applicable restrictions under other relevant Public Health Directions;  •	to provide assistance, care or support to an immediate family member.  https://web.archive.org/web/20200422004028/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/home-confinement-movement-gathering-direction
column69: Between the 15th and the 21st of April, any person who arrived in Queensland from another state or territory was not allowed to enter Queensland unless they were an exempt resident or an exempt person. An exempt resident or person was required to quarantine if they had been outside Australia or to a Covid-19 hotspot in the past 14 days. This policy came into effect at 12:01am on the 11th of April.  https://web.archive.org/web/20200421072852/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/border-restrictions
column79: The Queensland Government provided narrow relief in the form of a $200 rebate for all 2.1 million Queensland households (including the $50 Asset Ownership Dividend already announced) to offset the cost of water and electricity bills. column74: Australia’s borders are closed. Only Australian citizens, residents and immediate family members can travel to Australia. All travellers arriving in Australia by air or sea must be isolated in mandatory quarantine accommodation for 14 days from their arrival, with few exceptions.  https://web.archive.org/web/20200427015807/https://www.health.gov.au/news/health-alerts/novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov-health-alert/coronavirus-covid-19-advice-for-travellers
column77: 1. The Government’s JobKeeper Payment helped keep more Australians in jobs and support businesses affected by the significant economic impact of the coronavirus. Under the JobKeeper Payment, workers would receive a fortnightly payment of $1,500 (before tax) through their employer. The JobKeeper Payment was open to eligible businesses, not-for-profits and the self-employed who can enrol at ato.gov.au. The Payment is available from 30 March 2020 until 27 September 2020 with employers receiving the first payments from the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) from the first week of May.   2. The Government was temporarily expanding eligibility to income support payments and establishing a new, time-limited Coronavirus supplement to be paid at a rate of $550 per fortnight.  This would be paid to both existing and new recipients of the JobSeeker Payment, Youth Allowance jobseeker, Parenting Payment, Farm Household Allowance and Special Benefit. The Coronavirus supplement will be paid for the next 6 months. Eligible income support recipients will receive the full amount of the $550 Coronavirus supplement on top of their payment each fortnight.  As a continuation of current policies, this was labelled as 2F.  JobKeeper Payment: https://web.archive.org/web/20200421160551/https://treasury.gov.au/coronavirus/jobkeeper  “New, time-limited Coronavirus supplement”: https://web.archive.org/web/20220517043637/https://www.pm.gov.au/media/supporting-australian-workers-and-business

column15: There was no regional variation in State Government policies, which applied to the whole of Queensland:    According to a joint statement published by the Queensland Premier and Minister for Trade Annastacia Palaszczuk, and the Minister for Education and Minister for Industrial Relations Grace Grace on 13 April 2020, all students (except for children of essential workers and vulnerable students unable to learn from home) were required to learn from home.   These directions came into effect from 20 April 2020 and were expected to remain in place until 22 May 2020 at the earliest, so the restrictions in place between 22 and 29 April 2020 were a continuation of existing restrictions. column24: There was no regional variation in State Government policies, which applied to the whole of Queensland:    According to the Non-essential business, activity and undertaking Closure Direction (No.6), which came into effect on 21 April 2020, non-essential businesses, activities and undertakings were prohibited from operating.    The list of non-essential businesses included some retail food services, general retail, auction houses, personal care services, recreational and entertainment venues, and non-essential non-residential institutions.     However, there were numerous exceptions to these restrictions.   Food markets and farmers markets were allowed to operate, and hairdressers could operate according to a one person per four square metre rule.  Bottle shops and off-license premises attached to venues could operate under social distancing rules.  Residential facilities such as hostels and bed and breakfasts could operate for permanent residents, temporary residents (such as backpackers), and workers under social distancing and density rules.    The directions in place between 22-23 April 2020 were a continuation of existing directions    Archived link:  https://web.archive.org/web/20200730070203/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/revoked/non-essential-business-closure-direction-6
column33: There was no regional variation in State Government policies, which applied to the whole of Queensland:    According to the Home Confinement, Movement and Gathering Direction and the Home Confinement, Movement and Gathering Direction (No. 2), which came into effect on 2 April 2020 and 26 April 2020 respectively, gatherings were not permitted on non-residential premises. A maximum of two visitors (who were not workers, not present to support disabled individuals, and not the usual residents of the premises) were allowed in a residential premises at any one time.    Additionally, the Non-essential business, activity and undertaking Closure Direction (No.6), which came into effect on 21 April 2020, and the Non-essential business, activity and undertaking Closure Direction (No. 7), which came into effect on 24 April 2020, stated that non-essential businesses, activities and undertakings were prohibited from operating.    The list of non-essential businesses and undertakings included  some retail food services, general retail, auction houses, personal care services, recreational and entertainment venues, and non-essential non-residential institutions.     Cinemas, nightclubs, casinos and gambling venues, brothels, concert venues and arenas, zoos, galleries and historic sites were not permitted to continue in-person operations for the general public.    Weddings and other religious services could be held with a maximum of 5 people, and no more than 1 person per 4 square metres. Funerals could be held with a maximum of 10 people in addition to a maximum of 3 people conducting the service.    The restrictions in place between 22 and 29 April 2020 were a continuation of existing restrictions. column51: The State Government implemented COVID-Safe policies on public transport services across Queensland:    According to a media release published by the Queensland Minister for Transport and Main Roads Mark Bailey, which was published on 27 March 2020, some long haul train and coach services in regional Queensland were to be temporarily suspended or reduced from 30 March 2020 in response to COVID-19.    COVID-19 safety measures were also in place in South East Queensland and metropolitan public transport services.  According to a media released published by the Queensland Minister for Transport and Main Roads on 25 March 2020, passengers in South East Queensland were required to use cashless payment methods to pay for fares. Some bus operators closed seats adjacent to the driver and restricted entry and exit to rear doors in order to protect bus drivers.    The TransLink website (as of 18 April 2020) also stated that public transport vehicles across Queensland had their cleaning regimes increased to include daily sanitising. Queenslanders were advised to limit non-essential travel.    The measures in place between 22 and 29 April 2020 were a continuation of existing measures. column69: There was no regional variation in State Government policies, which applied to the whole of Queensland:    The Border Restrictions Direction (No.4) was in place between 10 April and 01 May 2020 in Queensland.    According to this Direction, individuals who arrived in Queensland from another State or Territory of Australia were prohibited from entering Queensland unless they had an exemption permitting them to enter.    Exemptions were granted to individuals performing essential work (such as providing emergency services or healthcare, performing essential duties for the military, police, or Government, performing specialist skills, or working with freight and logistics). They were also granted to individuals on compassionate grounds.    Exempt individuals who had been to a COVID-19 hotspot in the past 14 days were required to quarantine for 14 days unless they had visited the hotspot for an essential reason or were entering Queensland for an essential reason.    The directions in place between 22 and 29 April 2020 were a continuation of existing directions. column79: There was no regional variation in State Government policies, which applied to the whole of Queensland:    According to the Queensland Treasury website as of 29 April 2020 (which was last updated on 15 April 2020), the Queensland Government implemented a $200 rebate for Queensland households to assist with the costs of water and electricity bills during the COVID-19 pandemic.    The Queensland Government also implemented measures to assist individuals with rent and housing security.    Eligible land owners could apply for land tax relief which was required to be passed onto tenants. In order to be eligible for land tax relief, landlords were required to comply with principles which prevented tenants undergoing financial hardship from being evicted. Landlords receiving land tax relief were required to allow their tenants to refuse entry for non-essential reasons to limit the spread of COVID-19.  Residential tenants who were homeless or at risk of becoming homeless could receive a crisis payment of $500 a week for up to four weeks.    The measures in place between 22 and 29 April 2020 were a continuation of existing measures. column115: There was no regional variation in State Government policies, which applied to the whole of Queensland:    According to the Aged Care Direction (No.2), which was in effect in Queensland between 17 April and 8 May 2020, individuals were prohibited from entering a residential aged care facility unless they worked there, were providing essential supplies or services at the facility, were providing a care or support visit, were required to enter the facility for the purposes of law enforcement or emergency management, or were a prospective resident of the facility.    Individuals who had been to a place outside Australia or been in close contact with a COVID-19 case in the past 14 days, as well as individuals who had COVID-19 symptoms were prohibited from entering aged care facilities.    The directions in place between 22 and 29 April 2020 were a continuation of existing policies. column24: The Non-essential business, activity and undertaking Closure Direction (No. 7) came into effect from 8:48pm on 24 April 2020, replacing the  Non-essential business, activity and undertaking Closure Direction (No.6).  Under the new directions, residential facilities such as hostels, bed and breakfasts, short term rentals, and short term accommodation for leisure purposes could operate for individuals directed to self-quarantine by a relevant authority. Those requiring interim accommodation if their usual place of residence was unavailable, as well as essential workers away from their primary place of residence for a permitted purpose, could use residential facilities.  This was a relaxation of existing policies.    Other workplace restrictions remained the same:  non-essential businesses, activities and undertakings were prohibited from operating.    The list of non-essential businesses included some retail food services, general retail, auction houses, personal care services, recreational and entertainment venues, and non-essential non-residential institutions.     However, there were numerous exceptions to these restrictions.   Food markets and farmers markets were allowed to operate, and hairdressers could operate according to a one person per four square metre rule.  Bottle shops and off-license premises attached to venues could operate under social distancing rules.  Residential facilities such as hostels and bed and breakfasts could also operate for permanent residents, temporary residents (such as backpackers), and workers under social distancing and density rules.    Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20201029233528/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/revoked/non-essential-business-closure-direction-7  https://web.archive.org/web/20200730070203/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/revoked/non-essential-business-closure-direction-6

column74: As of 27 April 2020, Australia’s international border remains closed, since the Australian Government closed the border to all but non-citizens and non-residents on 20 March 2020. All travellers arriving in Australia by air or sea must be isolated in mandatory quarantine accommodation for 14 days from their arrival subject to few exceptions. These requirements will be managed and enforced by state and territory governments with Australian Government support, including from the Australian Defence Force and Australian Border Force.    This represents a 4 level of policy as of 27 April 2020 in Australia. column77: According to the Treasury, the JobKeeper Payment became available introduced from 30 March 2020 until 27 September 2020.    The JobKeeper Payment is a payment made to eligible businesses and not-for-profits affected by the Coronavirus to support them in retaining employees. Businesses must have paid their employees before they are entitled to receive the JobKeeper payment.     Where an employee’s total remuneration is less than $1,500 per fortnight (before tax), or has been stood down, the employer must provide the employee at least $1,500 per fortnight (before tax). Where an employee earns more than $1,500 per fortnight, employers can use the payment to subsidise the employee’s wages.    Self-employed individuals will also be eligible to receive the JobKeeper payment. Self-employed individuals are not informal workers as they operate their own business with an ABN in order to be eligible to the JobKeeper Payment. Therefore, this scheme was available to formal workers.    This represents a 2F level of policy as of 27 April 2020 in Australia.    Archived link:  https://web.archive.org/web/20220304125206/https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-04/JobKeeper_frequently_asked_questions_2.pdf

column51: This is a continuation of the existing policy. There are varying degrees of policy measures in different parts of Queensland, however, the variation is insignificant to change the ordinal value – thus coded ‘general’.     The majority of the long-haul train and coach services within Queensland were to be suspended or reduced from 30 March 2020 in response to Covid-19. see: https://web.archive.org/web/20220529025912/https://statements.qld.gov.au/statements/89598    Additional cleaning for SEQ public transport was introduced in mid-March which includes frequent sanitation in buses, trains, trams, and ferries. Queensland Rail was to boost its dedicated cleaning staff to ramp up regular cleaning measures and start a new disinfection process.   See: https://web.archive.org/web/20220313113722/https://statements.qld.gov.au/statements/89543    All public transport commuters in the south-east need to use a go card or pay for tickets using station fare machines since late March. Other measures such as blocking off the front row seats onboard vehicles and disabling the go car reader nearest driver have been in place to promote better social distancing. See: https://web.archive.org/web/20220529023942/https://statements.qld.gov.au/statements/89591    In a joint statement between the Queensland Premier and Minister of Transport, published on the government's official website on 25 April, the government announces a relief package to help operators and workers they employ continue running their service. This package is targeted to air, bus, and ferry services running in regional and remote communities with social distancing measures remain in place.   Regional buses are running as normal while regional aviation and ferries are at a reduced schedule.   See: https://web.archive.org/web/20220301015813/https://statements.qld.gov.au/statements/89737
column60: This is a continuation of the existing policy first introduced in March with no regional variation.    A person who resides in Queensland must not leave their principal place of residence except for, and only to the extent reasonably necessary to accomplish, unless for the following permitted reasons:  a.	to obtain food or other essential goods or services;  b.	to obtain medical treatment or other health care services;  c.	to engage in physical exercise, either alone or in the company of no more than one other person; or in the company of a family group who ordinarily live in the same household;  d.	to perform work on behalf of an employer that is engaged in an essential business, activity or undertaking, and the work to be performed is of a nature that cannot reasonably be performed from the person’s principal place of residence;  e.	to visit a terminally ill relative or to attend a funeral, subject to any applicable restrictions under other relevant Public Health Directions;  f.	to provide assistance, care or support to an immediate member of the person’s family;  g.	to attend any Court of Australia or to comply with or give effect to orders of the Court; or  h.	to attend a childcare facility, school, university, or other educational institution, to the extent care or instruction cannot reasonably be obtained in the person’s principal place of residence.  A person who leaves their residence for a permitted purpose may be accompanied by members of their household or, alternatively, by no more than one person who is not a member of their household.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220526050447/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/revoked/home-confinement-direction-1
column69: According to the Border Restriction Direction (no.4) published on 10 April (continuation of the existing policy), a person who arrives from other states & territories is not allowed to enter Queensland, unless they are an exempt resident/person.  An exempt resident/person who arrives in Queensland must self-quarantine if they have been outside Australia; or travel to hotspot areas in the last 14 days; or a person moving to Queensland to make Queensland their principal place of residence.   Exemptions were granted to individuals performing essential work (i.e., providing emergency services or healthcare, performing essential duties for the military, police, or Government, performing specialist skills, or working with freight and logistics). They were also granted to individuals on compassionate grounds.    Movement within Queensland is also prohibited as people are not allowed to leave their home unless for essential reasons – easing of restriction introduced on 1 May to allow people to leave home for recreations but need to stay within 50km radius from home.     No regional variation    https://web.archive.org/web/20220526064252/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/revoked/border-restrictions-4  https://web.archive.org/web/20210306042946/https://statements.qld.gov.au/statements/89738
column79: This is a continuation of the existing policy that came into effect in April with no regional variation.   On 24 April, The Queensland Government enacted the National Cabinet’s moratorium on evictions and published the Residential Tenancies Practice Guide, which formalised temporary arrangements and protections for tenancies impacted by COVID-19 for the next six months.   Tenants who are suffering or who have suffered excessive hardship because of COVID-19 who cannot meet their rent commitments cannot be evicted or listed in a tenancy database because of that suffering.   The practice guide would help property owners and their tenants in their discussions to negotiate a way through the next six months.     Additionally, the government also provides rebate Queensland households to offset the cost of water and electrical bills (as published on the Queensland government's official website – last update on 15 April)    As there is no reference to the contract type, it is assumed that the above arrangements apply to all contracts, thus the code 2.     https://web.archive.org/web/20200429081551/https://www.treasury.qld.gov.au/programs-and-policies/covid19-package/  https://web.archive.org/web/20220526104638/https://statements.qld.gov.au/statements/89733  https://web.archive.org/web/20220526104655/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp2021/Chronologies/COVID-19StateTerritoryGovernmentAnnouncements

column90: Based on the government media release on 24 April, the Attorney-General stated that 500 more public servants would be trained to be ready to enhance contact tracing with public health units across Queensland. Queensland contact tracing efforts involve measures to ensure those in quarantine stay in quarantine, which includes: 3410 random telephone calls, 2000 text messages, 158 home visits (as part of weekly blitz)  see: https://web.archive.org/web/20220531052632/https://statements.qld.gov.au/statements/89730    Additionally, based on the written submission to the inquiry into the Queensland health response to Covid-19, dated 17 June 2020, The Queensland Health claimed that they have had the capacity to commence contact tracing and outbreak response within four hours of a first confirmed case being notified to the relevant jurisdictional authority. Public Health physicians were available 24 hours per day to assist with contact tracing. Queensland Health and primary health services have telehealth/video conferencing capabilities to support an outbreak response.   See: https://web.archive.org/web/20220528114947/https://documents.parliament.qld.gov.au/committees/HCDSDFVPC/2020/COVID-19/bp-17Jun2020.pdf    Around the period, there is evidence of the flatting of the curve (less than 5 daily new cases). column115: According to the Aged Care Direction (no. 2) published on 14 April (continuation of the existing policy), a person must not enter, or remain on, the premises of a residential aged care facility unless an employee or contractor or is providing specific permitted supports or purposes such as essential supplies or services at the facility, medical or care or support visit, end of life support, and emergency management.  An authorised person must not enter the premises if:  -	they have a temperature higher than 38 degrees celsius or symptoms of acute respiratory infection, or   -	has been in contact with a known positive case within the previous 14 days or has been to a place outside Queensland during the 14 days immediately preceding entry, or  -	the person is aged under 16 years except in special circumstances   An operator must not permit a resident, excluding an end of life resident, to leave the facility except to receive or access health care or in the case of emergency. column24: On 1 May, the government releases an updated Non-essential business, activities and undertaking closure direction (No.8) and revoked the previous direction (7).   Under the new direction, easing of restrictions on several business/workplace settings is introduced such as:  -	Real estate auctions and open house inspections may be conducted with a maximum of 6 people including the real estate agent inside the building at any one time.   -	Beauty therapy including cosmetic injections, tanning, waxing and nail salons provided by the registered health practitioners are permitted to open  -	Personal appearance services where skin penetration is used (e.g., tattoo parlours, body piercing) can open if provided by the registered health practitioners  -	Drive-in cinemas with members of a person’s household are permitted. People should remain in their vehicles to the extent possible.   -	Hostels, bed and breakfasts, backpackers, boarding houses, short term rentals/accommodations that are open for the specific permitted reasons must have a health management plan and must operate in compliance with the health management plan (unless the facility operates solely for permanent residents of the facility or health and community services) starting from 5 May.   All the above are subject to social distancing measurement to the extent possible and/or no more than one person per 4 square metres rule.     Other workplace restrictions remained the same.   No regional variation.     https://web.archive.org/web/20220526033653/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/revoked/non-essential-business-closure-direction-8

column74: Determination: No Change – Continuation of Current Policy    Policy Information: This is a continuation of the existing policy that took effect on 20 March 2020. Australian National government is closing its border to all non-citizens and non-residents. Exemption only for Australian citizens, permanent residents and their immediate family, including spouses, legal guardians and dependants. New Zealand citizens who live in Australia as Australian residents are also exempt, as are New Zealanders transiting to New Zealand. Exemptions for Pacific Islanders transiting to their home countries will continue to apply. Australian citizens and permanent residents and those exempt from our entry restrictions will continue to be subject to a strict 14 days of self-isolation. column115: According to the Aged Care Direction (No. 3), a person cannot enter an aged care facility, unless:   - the person is an employee or contractor of the residential aged care facility; or  - the person's presence at the premises is for the purposes of providing goods or services that are necessary for the effective operation of the residential aged care facility, whether the goods or services are provided for consideration or on a voluntary basis; or  - the person's presence at the premises is for the purposes of providing health, medical, personal care, or pharmaceutical services to a resident of the residential aged care facility, whether the goods or services are provided for consideration or on a voluntary basis; or  - the person's presence at the premises is for the purposes of a care and support visit to a resident of the residential aged care facility on a particular day, and is the only care and support visit made to the resident on that day; or  - the person's presence at the premises is for the purposes of end of life support for a resident of the residential aged care facility; or  - the person's presence at the premises is required for the purposes of emergency management, law enforcement or the exercise of a power or function of a government agency or entity under a law; or  - the person's presence at the premises is in the person's capacity as a prospective resident of the residential aged care facility.    https://web.archive.org/web/20200512121332/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/aged-care

column74: This is a continuation of the existing policy that has been in effect since 20 March 2020. The National government is closing its border to all non-citizens and non-residents. column88: This is a continuation of the existing policy.  As published on the DoH website (last updated on 2 April), the national government provides general guidelines for who can be tested that is those that develop fever or respiratory symptoms and meet at least one of the following criteria:  •	you have returned from overseas in the past 14 days  •	you have been in close contact with someone diagnosed with COVID-19 in the past 14 days  •	you travelled on a cruise ship (either passenger or crew) in the 14 days before developing symptoms  •	you are a health care, aged care or residential care worker  •	you have lived in an area where there is a higher risk of community transmission, as defined by the local public health unit  Or they should also be tested if meeting all the following criteria:   •	you are in hospital  •	you have fever and serious respiratory symptoms  •	there is no other clear cause of the symptoms  People in high-risk settings (e.g., aged & residential care facilities) will be tested if there are 2 or more people with fever and respiratory symptoms in the setting.  Some states and territories may have more testing criteria based on their cases.    https://web.archive.org/web/20200402205514/https://www.health.gov.au/news/health-alerts/novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov-health-alert/what-you-need-to-know-about-coronavirus-covid-19    However, on 24 April, National Cabinet agreed to expand testing criteria across Australia to all people with mild symptoms of COVID-19. column115: During this time period, there were extensive protections placed by the state government for residential aged care facilities. Under the Aged Care Direction (No.3), individuals were not allowed on the premises of an aged care facility unless they were:  -an employee or contractor of facility  -required for purposes of providing essential goods and services necessary for effective operation of aged care facility  -there for purposes of providing health, medical or personal care or pharmaceutical products to residents  -there for purposes of care and support visit to resident on that particular day  -there for purposes of providing end of life support for resident  -required for purposes of emergency management, law enforcement or exercise of power or function of government agency  -there for purposes of being prospective resident.    However, if any of the following conditions apply, the individual must not be allowed to enter or remain on premises until end of public health emergency:  -person arrived to Australia from overseas in past 14 days  -person had known contact with confirmed COVID-19 case in past 14 days  -person has temperature equal or higher than 38 degrees or has acute respiratory infection  -person is aged under 16 years, other than in circumstances where person's presence is for end of life support  -does not have up to date influenza vaccination if available to person.    https://web.archive.org/web/20200512121332/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/aged-care

column69: As published on QLD government website, only Queensland residents, residents of border communities undertaking essential activities and those considered an ‘exempt person’ are allowed to enter Queensland via air, sea, rail or road from another State or Territory.    If you meet the criteria for an ‘exempt person’ (see below for more details—‘Who is allowed to enter Queensland?’), then please consider applying online for a Queensland Entry Pass to avoid delays at the border.    Even if a person is a Queensland resident, resident of a border community or an exempt person, they must self-quarantine if they have been in a declared COVID-19 hotspot in Australia in the last 14 days, unless they were in the hotspot for an essential purpose, like going to a funeral, or they need to enter Queensland again for an essential purpose, for example to work.    People moving to Queensland to take up permanent residence will be allowed to enter, but will also be required to self-quarantine for 14 days, which could be at the new residential address.    If a person is entering Queensland from another State or Territory by air in order to transfer to another flight, they are allowed to enter Queensland, but must remain in the airport until the time of a transfer to another flight, or self-quarantine in a hotel until the other flight or follow the direction of the relevant authorities and self-quarantine at a nominated premises, for example if a return flight is not available the same day.   This represents continuation in the COVID-19 policy response.   https://web.archive.org/web/20200527174822/https://www.covid19.qld.gov.au/government-actions/border-closing

column77: Median weekly earnings were $1,209.00 for all employees, and the JobKeeper Payment was greater than 50% median salary.  The JobKeeper Payment helps businesses significantly impacted by the Coronavirus cover the costs of their employees’ wages, so more Australians can retain their jobs and continue to earn an income. Employers will notify employees if they are claiming the fortnightly payment of $1,500. The first payments were made in the week commencing 4 May 2020.  Since 27 April 2020 the Government has temporarily expanded eligibility to income support payments and established a new, time-limited Coronavirus supplement to be paid at a rate of $550 per fortnight. Indoor events with 500-10,000 people must comply with a COVID Safe Event Plan.  Indoor events with over 10,000 people must have a COVID Safe Event plan approved by the Chief Health Officer.   Outdoor events less than 1000 people must comply with a COVID Safe Event Checklist.   Outdoor events with 1,000 to 10,000 people must comply with a COVID Safe Event Plan approved by local public health units.   Outdoor events with over 10,000 people must comply with a COVID Safe Event approved by the Chief Health Officer.   Other venues must comply and have an approved plan allowing for capacity of up to 50% of seated venue capacity or 1 person per 4 square metres for indoor venues (whatever is greater).   Outdoor venues are allowed up to 75% of seated venue capacity.   Major sport facilities, which are indoor, are allowed up to 25,000 spectators or 50% of seated venue capacity.   Major sport facilities, which are outdoor, up to 75% of seated venue capacity.   Cleaning should be heightened  and the  entry, exit and flow of visitors should be managed carefully.  This represents a continuance of the policy and is in place across QLD. There does not appear to be any variation due to vaccination status.   https://web.archive.org/web/20201026163523/https://www.health.qld.gov.au/system-governance/legislation/cho-public-health-directions-under-expanded-public-health-act-powers/business-activity-undertaking-direction"
column42: "As at 16 November 2020, there are  measures in place for gatherings.   Social distancing must be in place  at events allowing only 1 person per 4 square meters indoors, 1 person per 2 square metres outdoors, at most 50 people if indoor floor space is less than 200 square metres.  For personal (non-event) gatherings, up to 40 people are allowed in homes and public spaces across QLD. This includes weddings.   This represents a continuance of the policy. It is in place across QLD  https://web.archive.org/web/20201027202925/https://www.covid19.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0016/127150/DPC7309-COVID-19-Restrictions-roadmap.pdf?nocache-v8  https://web.archive.org/web/20201101144948/https://www.qld.gov.au/health/conditions/health-alerts/coronavirus-covid-19/current-status/public-health-directions/business-activity"
column51: "As at 16 November 2020, there are recommendations in place. People are recommended to only use transport if necessary and if they are feeling well.   The recommendations include:  -Try to plan ahead to avoid peak hours  -Keep distance between yourself and other passengers by:  -standing away from others while at a stop or platform  -leaving space between you and the person in front as you enter the vehicle  -sitting away from other people  -waiting for a later service   - always following staff advice.  -Use contactless payment methods like go cards.  -Minimise contact with surfaces like handles and doors.  -Carry hand sanitiser to clean your hands before and after using public transport.  -Consider wearing a face mask in situations where you are unable to maintain social (physical) distance.  -If you are unwell please stay home and contact your doctor for advice.        This is in place across QLD. This represents a continuation of the policy.  https://web.archive.org/web/20201104210748/https://www.qld.gov.au/health/conditions/health-alerts/coronavirus-covid-19/protect-yourself-others/coronavirus-prevention"

column69: "As at 16 November 2020, there are  requirements for interstate travellers.   Travellers are not recommended to travel if they are unwell.   People who have been in a COVID-19 hotspot within the last 14 days are not allowed in except if they are needed in QLD for essential activities. Currently, all of Victoria and some of NSW are hotspots.   A QLD Border Declaration Pass is required before entering with a test for COVID-19 also required if any symptoms develop.   Residents in QLD can return to QLD but must quarantine if they were in a COVID-19 hotspot in the last 14 days.   These measures are in place across QLD and represent a continuance of the policy.  https://web.archive.org/web/20201108164048/https://www.qld.gov.au/health/conditions/health-alerts/coronavirus-covid-19/current-status/public-health-directions/border-restrictions"

column115: "As at 16 November 2020, there are restrictions on visits to high risk settings.  Residential aged care facilities will not allow any visitors if they are waiting on a COVID-19 test result.   Residents are allowed up to two visitors at one time. Service providers may visit the facility such as hairdressers, legal advisors, mental health providers and allied health providers.   Visitors should socially distance where possible and stay away if unwell. Visitors cannot be someone who is   -is unwell  - has returned from overseas in the last 14 days  - has had contact with a person with COVID-19 in the last 14 days  - has travelled to a COVID-19 hotspot in the last 14 days   -has been tested for COVID-19 and is waiting for the result   -has COVID-19 symptoms (Opens in new window) of fever (37.5 degrees or more), cough, shortness of breath, sore throat, loss of smell or taste, runny nose, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting or fatigue.  - has not had the 2020 flu vaccination (unless it is unavailable to you).
