column90: VIC Gov has been implementing contact tracing as one of the critical components of its approach to containing the spread of Covid-19.   The VIC contact tracing system involves interviewing confirmed cases, calling their close contact, checking up on those in isolation and investing links between individual cases and possible clusters. However, there are evidence that Victoria’s contact-tracing system was overwhelmed and deemed ineffective in responding to the rising covid cases during the second wave that started in June. Based on a news report published on 14/12/2020, Parliamentary inquiry findings revealed that: “Victorian Government's stubborn reluctance to embrace a new contact tracing system when it was needed was a "failure" which cost lives during the state's deadly second wave”. column90: VIC Gov has been implementing contact tracing as one of the critical components of its approach to containing the spread of Covid-19.   The VIC contact tracing system involves interviewing confirmed cases, calling their close contact, checking up on those in isolation and investing links between individual cases and possible clusters. column115: From 11:59pm on Sunday 22 November restrictions are changing for visits to care facilities in Victoria.  There are no limits on the purpose of visits, the number of visitors or the length of the visit. Visits to people living in care facilities are no longer limited by Chief Health Officer directions. Visitors will need to follow visiting rules set by the facility. People of any age can visit people in care facilities. Do not visit someone in a care facility if you are feeling unwell. Visitors to any care facility across Victoria must wear a face mask, unless they have a lawful reason for not doing so. All personal care workers, including hairdressers and barbers, can visit care facilities to provide hairdressing services to residents. column74: According to a joint media released published by the Australian Minister for Health and the Chief Medical Officer published on 2 March 2020, healthcare and residential aged care workers arriving in Australia from Italy and South Korea were asked not to attend work for 14 days after arriving in Australia. This was an escalation of public health advice directed towards individuals arriving from Italy and South Korea.    Existing travel restrictions imposed on individuals arriving from China and Iran remained the same:  Foreign nationals who had been in Iran or China within the past 14 days were prohibited from entering Australia. Australian citizens, permanent residents and immediate family members who had been in Iran or China in the past 14 days were required to quarantine at home for 14 days after arriving in Australia.     Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20220121004113/https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22media%2Fpressrel%2F7216775%22  https://web.archive.org/web/20220121011945/https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22media%2Fpressrel%2F7218407%22

According to a joint media release from the Australian Prime Minister, the Minister for Health, and the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Minister for Women, foreign nationals who had been in the Republic of Korea on or after 5 March 2020 were prohibited from entering Australia for 14 days from the time they had left or transited through Korea. Australian citizens, permanent residents and immediate family members who had been in Iran in the past 14 days were required to quarantine at home for 14 days after arriving in Australia.   Enhanced health screening and temperature checking arrangements were implemented for individuals arriving in Australia from Italy during this time.    This was a tightening of measures imposed on individuals arriving from the Republic of Korea and Italy. Existing travel restrictions imposed on individuals arriving from China and Iran remained the same:  Foreign nationals who had been in Iran or China within the past 14 days were prohibited from entering Australia. Australian citizens, permanent residents and immediate family members who had been in Iran or China in the past 14 days were required to quarantine at home for 14 days after arriving in Australia.     Archived links:  https://web.archive.org/web/20220121001025/https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22media%2Fpressrel%2F7223641%22  https://web.archive.org/web/20220121011945/https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22media%2Fpressrel%2F7218407%22

As published on the Department of Home Affairs website, The Australian Government announced on 12 March 2020 that travel restrictions will continue to apply to travellers arriving from any part of mainland China, Iran, Republic of Korea and Italy.    Foreign nationals (excluding permanent residents of Australia) who have been in the following countries will not be allowed to enter Australia for 14 days from the time they have left or transited through:  mainland China  Iran  Republic of Korea  Italy.  Australian citizens and permanent residents will still be able to enter, as will their immediate family members (spouses, legal guardians or dependants only). They will be required to self-isolate at home for 14 days from the day they left China, Iran, the Republic of Korea or Italy.  Australia will deny entry to anyone who has left or transited a country subject to travel restrictions within the previous 14 days, with the exception of:  Australian citizens  permanent residents  New Zealand citizens resident in Australia  immediate family members of Australian citizens and permanent residents including spouses, minor dependants and legal guardians diplomats.  This represents a continuation of the policy response.  https://web.archive.org/web/20200314024611/https://www.homeaffairs.gov.au/news-media/current-alerts/novel-coronavirus

column77: According to the Treasury, the JobKeeper Payment became available introduced from 30 March 2020 until 27 September 2020.    The JobKeeper Payment is a payment made to eligible businesses and not-for-profits affected by the Coronavirus to support them in retaining employees. Businesses must have paid their employees before they are entitled to receive the JobKeeper payment.     Where an employee’s total remuneration is less than $1,500 per fortnight (before tax), or has been stood down, the employer must provide the employee at least $1,500 per fortnight (before tax). Where an employee earns more than $1,500 per fortnight, employers can use the payment to subsidise the employee’s wages.    Self-employed individuals will also be eligible to receive the JobKeeper payment. Self-employed individuals are not informal workers as they operate their own business with an ABN in order to be eligible to the JobKeeper Payment. Therefore, this scheme was available to formal workers.    This represents a 2F level of policy as of 27 April 2020 in Australia.    Archived link:  https://web.archive.org/web/20220304125206/https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-04/JobKeeper_frequently_asked_questions_2.pdf

column115: Under the Visitors to Residential Aged Care Facilities Directions #2, in force since 25 April 2020, most non-residents are banned from entering aged care facilities. Exceptions include:  -	people who work at the facility (officers, employees, and contractors)  -	people providing essential goods and services to the facility  -	people providing health care or medicine to a resident  -	people visiting a resident to provide care and support (for up to 2 hours) or end-of-life support (e.g. religious or spiritual services)  -	emergency and law enforcement officials (e.g. police officers, ambulance staff, firefighters)  -	lawyers providing will or estate planning services to residents  -	prospective residents of the facility    Even if they belong to one of the categories allowed to enter, people must not enter aged care facilities if they:  -	have been outside Australia in the past 14 days  -	have been in contact with a confirmed COVID-19 case in the past 14 days  -	have respiratory symptoms or a fever higher than 38 degrees  -	are not vaccinated against influenza (unless they are emergency/law enforcement officials)  -	are under 16 years old, unless providing end-of-life support to a resident    This is a continuation of policy since 25th April 2020, and applies statewide with no regional variation.  See http://web.archive.org/web/20220913085505/https://www.wa.gov.au/system/files/2020-07/Revoked-Visitors-to-Residential-Aged-Care-Facilities-Directions-No2_0.pdf

column77: On 22 March (this is a continuation of the existing policy), the National government introduces economic support packages in response to the covid-19 pandemic which includes support for workers and households. column115: Under the Visitors to Residential Aged Care Facilities Directions #2, in force since 25 April 2020, most non-residents are banned from entering aged care facilities. Exceptions include:  -	people who work at the facility (officers, employees, and contractors)  -	people providing essential goods and services to the facility  -	people providing health care or medicine to a resident  -	people visiting a resident to provide care and support (for up to 2 hours) or end-of-life support (e.g. religious or spiritual services)  -	emergency and law enforcement officials (e.g. police officers, ambulance staff, firefighters)  -	lawyers providing will or estate planning services to residents  -	prospective residents of the facility    Even if they belong to one of the categories allowed to enter, people must not enter aged care facilities if they:  -	have been outside Australia in the past 14 days  -	have been in contact with a confirmed COVID-19 case in the past 14 days  -	have respiratory symptoms or a fever higher than 38 degrees  -	are not vaccinated against influenza (unless they are emergency/law enforcement officials)  -	are under 16 years old, unless providing end-of-life support to a resident    This is a continuation of policy since 25th April 2020, and applies statewide with no regional variation.  See http://web.archive.org/web/20220913085505/https://www.wa.gov.au/system/files/2020-07/Revoked-Visitors-to-Residential-Aged-Care-Facilities-Directions-No2_0.pdf

column15: All students returned to in-person schooling from Monday, May 18, 2020. column74: International Travel Restrictions    The National Cabinet noted the AHPPC’s advice on high-risk countries for COVID-19 importation risk and its continued support for the 14 day self isolation requirement for all returning travellers.  The National Cabinet welcomed the Commonwealth Government’s decision to stop the entry of non-citizens and non-permanent residents and their immediate families into Australia after 9pm AEDT on Friday 20 March 2020 in order to align international travel restrictions with the risks. column115: Under the Visitors to Residential Aged Care Facilities Directions #2, in force since 25 April 2020, most non-residents are banned from entering aged care facilities. Exceptions include:  -	people who work at the facility (officers, employees, and contractors)  -	people providing essential goods and services to the facility  -	people providing health care or medicine to a resident  -	people visiting a resident to provide care and support (for up to 2 hours) or end-of-life support (e.g. religious or spiritual services)  -	emergency and law enforcement officials (e.g. police officers, ambulance staff, firefighters)  -	lawyers providing will or estate planning services to residents  -	prospective residents of the facility    Even if they belong to one of the categories allowed to enter, people must not enter aged care facilities if they:  -	have been outside Australia in the past 14 days  -	have been in contact with a confirmed COVID-19 case in the past 14 days  -	have respiratory symptoms or a fever higher than 38 degrees  -	are not vaccinated against influenza (unless they are emergency/law enforcement officials)  -	are under 16 years old, unless providing end-of-life support to a resident    This is a continuation of policy since 25th April 2020, and applies statewide with no regional variation.  See http://web.archive.org/web/20220913085505/https://www.wa.gov.au/system/files/2020-07/Revoked-Visitors-to-Residential-Aged-Care-Facilities-Directions-No2_0.pdf

column74: International Travel Restrictions    The National Cabinet noted the AHPPC’s advice on high-risk countries for COVID-19 importation risk and its continued support for the 14 day self isolation requirement for all returning travellers.  The National Cabinet welcomed the Commonwealth Government’s decision to stop the entry of non-citizens and non-permanent residents and their immediate families into Australia after 9pm AEDT on Friday 20 March 2020 in order to align international travel restrictions with the risks. column77: Continuation of policy from Mar 22, 2020 where the Australian Government announced a second economic support package, bringing additional support of around $66 billion. The WA Department of Health only encourages people to stay home if unwell (link 2).  https://web.archive.org/web/20210509095432/https://www.mediastatements.wa.gov.au/Pages/McGowan/2020/06/WA-ready-for-the-next-phase-of-the-COVID-19-roadmap.aspx  https://web.archive.org/web/20201019203635/https://healthywa.wa.gov.au/Articles/A_E/Coronavirus
column79: As of 28 Nov 2020, the WA Government continues to provide broad debt/contract relief across WA (link 1). These include a freeze on increases to all household fees and charges, no utility disconnections, doubling of the Energy Assistance Payment, alternative tax payment arrangements, amongst other relief. Around 1.1 million Synergy and Horizon Power customers will also receive a one-off $600 credit, effective as of October 4 2020.  A 6-month moratorium on residential tenancy evictions became law in April 2020 to prevent tenants having to move out or becoming homeless during the COVID-19 pandemic. The moratorium period began 30 March, 2020, and was extended to 28 March 2021 (link 2). During the moratorium period, rent cannot be increased, expiring fixed-term tenancies automatically convert to periodical tenancies, and tenants who end a fixed-term tenancy before its end date due to COVID-19 related financial hardship will not incur break lease fees (but will still be liable for damage and rent arrears).  https://web.archive.org/web/20201029104655/https://www.wa.gov.au/organisation/department-of-the-premier-and-cabinet/covid-19-coronavirus-western-australian-government-response#household-support  https://web.archive.org/web/20201231004753/https://www.wa.gov.au/organisation/department-of-the-premier-and-cabinet/covid-19-coronavirus-western-australian-government-response
column86: As of 28 Nov 2020, there continues to be coordinated public campaign for COVID-19 across WA, evidenced by the frequent, consistent updates to WA's coronavirus website.  Archived weblink: https://web.archive.org/web/20201023210707/https://www.wa.gov.au/government/covid-19-coronavirus
column88: As of 28 Nov 2020, the testing policy across WA continues to be anyone symptomatic. The WA Government continues to urge anyone experiencing any flu-like symptoms to get tested.  Archived weblink: https://web.archive.org/web/20201019203635/https://healthywa.wa.gov.au/Articles/A_E/Coronavirus
column90: As of 28 Nov 2020, there continues to be comprehensive contact tracing across WA. WA's Department of Health continues to post all locations of confirmed cases and contacts any close contacts.  Archived weblink: https://web.archive.org/web/20201031035051/https://healthywa.wa.gov.au/Articles/A_E/Coronavirus/Locations-visited-by-confirmed-cases
column103: As of 28 Nov 2020, there continues to be no face mask policy across WA. WA’s Department of Health does not recommend face mask use, although it concedes that masks offer some protection when physical distancing is not possible or in high transmission situations.    Archived weblink:  https://web.archive.org/web/20201016063626/https://ww2.health.wa.gov.au/~/media/Files/Corporate/general%20documents/Infectious%20diseases/PDF/Coronavirus/coronavirus-faqs.pdf#page=7
column106: As of 28 Nov 2020, there continues to be no availability of COVID-19 vaccines across WA. The first COVID-19 vaccines were administered in Australia on 22 Feb 2021.  Archived weblink: https://web.archive.org/web/20220623120120/https://www.health.gov.au/news/first-covid-19-vaccinations-in-australia
column115: As of 28 Nov 2020, there continues to be narrow protections of elderly people across WA. On 18 Sep 2020, the WA Government announced that people may not enter an aged care facility if they: have returned from overseas in the past 14 days, have been notified as being a close contact in the past 14 days, have any COVID-19 symptoms, or have not had an up-to-date influenza vaccine.  Archived weblink: https://web.archive.org/web/20201003055507/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-09/Visitors-to-Residential-Aged-Care-Facilities-Directions-No-4.pdf

column74: As published on the Department of Home Affairs website, no foreign arrivals are permitted into the country unless they are in an exempt category or have been granted an individual exemption which includes compassionate and national interest grounds. All international arrivals must quarantine for 14 days at a designated facility. There is the possibility to travel to Australia quarantine free without an exemption if you have been in New Zealand for 14 days or more and not been in a designated COVID-19 outbreak location, and you are travelling to Australia on a quarantine-free flight from 16/10/2020.    https://web.archive.org/web/20201130233418/https://covid19.homeaffairs.gov.au/travel-restrictions    https://web.archive.org/web/20201130222312/https://covid19.homeaffairs.gov.au/new-zealand-safe-travel-zone
column77: The Government has extended the payment period of its temporary Coronavirus Supplement from 1 January 2021 to 31 March 2021. The amount of the Coronavirus Supplement has been adjusted for this period to reflect the gradually improving economic conditions. From 25 September 2020 to 31 December 2020, the Supplement amount will continue to be $250 per fortnight. Both existing and new recipients of eligible payments will continue to be paid the Coronavirus Supplement.     https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-11/Fact_sheet-Income_Support_for_Individuals.pdf

column15: As published on the Western Australian Government’s Media Statements page on 22 June 2020, the state moved to phase 4 of the WA roadmap to relax COVID-restrictions. As part of this policy change, the previous limit of 100 students was lifted. Accordingly, school attendance is mandatory for all students, except those who are medically vulnerable or who have medically-vulnerable family members. Schools will still continue to follow appropriate risk assessment procedures. This was implemented across WA on 27 June 2020. The policy remained in force as of 1 December 2020.     https://web.archive.org/web/20210921105901/https://www.mediastatements.wa.gov.au/Pages/McGowan/2020/06/WA-ready-for-the-next-phase-of-the-COVID-19-roadmap.aspx    https://web.archive.org/web/20210511015917/https://www.wa.gov.au/organisation/department-of-the-premier-and-cabinet/covid-19-coronavirus-education-and-family-advice
column24: As published on the Western Australian Government’s Media Statements page on 22 June 2020, the state moved to phase 4 of the WA roadmap to relax COVID-restrictions. This lessening of restrictions was aimed particularly at a number of food, entertainment and fitness businesses. The policy included provisions: removing seated service requirements at food businesses; allowing unseated performances at venues such as concert halls, live music venues, bars, pubs and nightclubs; permitting gyms to operate unstaffed, with regular cleaning maintained; and enabling a casino gaming floor reopening under agreed temporary restrictions. Further, WA businesses are expected to ensure they complete and update COVID Safety Plans. This was implemented across WA on 27 June 2020. The policy remained in force as of 1 December 2020.     https://web.archive.org/web/20210921105901/https://www.mediastatements.wa.gov.au/Pages/McGowan/2020/06/WA-ready-for-the-next-phase-of-the-COVID-19-roadmap.aspx    https://web.archive.org/web/20210921120342/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-06/Phase-4-roadmap.pdf
column33: All events with 500 or more people in attendance must follow a COVID Event Plan, which outlines precautions taken to mitigate the risk of COVID transmission (e.g. social distancing, hygiene and disinfection, and keeping a register of patrons for contact tracing purposes) and have the COVID plan approved by local government authorities. Such events must also be registered on the WA Department of Health's Events Register.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210510232147/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-10/COVID-Event-Guidelines.pdf (COVID plan guidelines)    http://web.archive.org/web/20210906082241/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-12/Closure_and_Restriction_Limit_the_Spread_Directions_No_8.pdf (gathering regulations for 1-4 Dec)
column42: Gatherings of 500 or more people must be registered with the Department of Health, and must follow a COVID-19 safety plan which has been approved by local government authorities.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210510232147/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-10/COVID-Event-Guidelines.pdf    Both indoor and outdoor gatherings (of 2 people or more) must generally maintain at least 2 square metres of space per person. Seated entertainment venues and houses of worship do not have to comply with the requirement for 2 square metres per person, provided they allow no more than 60% of seated capacity, and ensure that patrons remain at least 1.5 metres apart where possible. Beauty services (e.g. hairdressers, tattoo parlours, nail salons) do not have to comply with the requirement for 2 square metres per person, but must keep patrons at least 1.5 metres apart.  http://web.archive.org/web/20210906082241/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-12/Closure_and_Restriction_Limit_the_Spread_Directions_No_8.pdf
column51: As published on the Transperth website on 31 July 2020, the WA Government has decided to allow public transport to remain functioning. Small adjustments have been made to: limit the handling of cash, increase environmental cleaning, timetabling all available vehicles during periods of peak demand and encouraging passengers to socially distance themselves as much as possible. These guidelines were updated in July and were still current during December of 2020    https://web.archive.org/web/20201125100825/https://www.transperth.wa.gov.au/Using-Transperth/coronavirus-advice
column60: As published on the Western Australian Government’s Media Statements page on 22 June 2020, the state moved to phase 4 of the WA roadmap to relax COVID-restrictions. As a result, no stay at home order was imposed and all existing limits to gatherings were lifted, the only caveat being that individuals should abide by WA's reduced 2sqm rule.     https://web.archive.org/web/20210509095432/https://www.mediastatements.wa.gov.au/Pages/McGowan/2020/06/WA-ready-for-the-next-phase-of-the-COVID-19-roadmap.aspx
column69: A controlled interstate border is in place effective 14 November 2020. States and territories are assigned a risk level based on current levels of COVID-19 community transmission; travellers arriving in WA are subject to varying levels of restrictions based on the risk level of the state they are travelling from.  All travellers, including those from "very low risk" states and territories, are required to complete a G2G Pass and undergo a health screening upon arrival.    ACT, NT, QLD, TAS are classified as "very low risk". NSW and VIC are classified as "low risk". Travellers are permitted to enter WA without an exemption, but must self-quarantine for 14 days.  http://web.archive.org/web/20201101003915/https://www.wa.gov.au/government/announcements/controlled-interstate-border    Effective November 16, 2020, South Australia is classified as "medium risk". Travellers from SA are not permitted to enter without an exemption, and must self-quarantine for 14 days.  http://web.archive.org/web/20201201013252/https://www.wa.gov.au/government/announcements/additional-stricter-controls-sa-arrivals

column77: On 16 March 2020, the WA State Government announced and implemented a $607 million stimulus package to support WA households and small businesses. Part of this announcement was the policy change enabling small businesses that pay payroll tax to receive a one-off grant of $17,500. Further, the $1 million payroll tax threshold was brought forward by six months to July 1, 2020. This policy was still in force on 1 December 2020.     https://web.archive.org/web/20210922133553/https://www.mediastatements.wa.gov.au/Pages/McGowan/2020/03/COVID-19-economic-response-Relief-for-businesses-and-households.aspx    https://web.archive.org/web/20210922132135/https://www.wa.gov.au/government/multi-step-guides/payroll-tax-employer-guide/covid-19-relief-payroll-tax-employer-guide    https://web.archive.org/web/20210511115745/https://www.wa.gov.au/organisation/department-of-the-premier-and-cabinet/covid-19-coronavirus-support-business
column79: The WA State Government Implemented the Residential Rent Relief Grant Scheme on 1 May 2020. The State Government allocated $30 million to provide one-off rent relief payments equivalent to four weeks’ rent (capped at $2,000) to eligible Western Australians experiencing financial hardship due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The scheme is available to tenants or sub-tenants who have lost their job, applied to Centrelink for income support, have less than $10,000 in savings, and are still paying at least 25% of their income in rent. Phase two of this scheme remained operational on 1 December 2020 and ended at the end of the month.     https://web.archive.org/web/20210708033717/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-05/covid-19-state-government-support-for-tenants-and-landlords-fact-sheet.pdf    https://web.archive.org/web/20211004021522/https://www.commerce.wa.gov.au/publications/covid-19-relief-grant-will-help-pay-rent-debt-landlords-bulletin-issue-50
column86: Since early 2020, the WA government has provided information, advice, news, and resources regarding COVID-19 to the West Australian community through its official websites. As of December 2020, these websites were still active and regularly updated.  https://web.archive.org/web/20201230013801/https://www.wa.gov.au/government/covid-19-coronavirus  https://web.archive.org/web/20210105164000/https://ww2.health.wa.gov.au/Articles/A_E/Coronavirus     Additionally, from November 2020 to January 2021, the government ran a public information campaign urging West Australians to maintain COVID-safe practices (such as social distancing, hand washing, and getting tested if sick) during the summer. This campaign included outdoor signs, posters, social media posts, and radio advertising.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210511021623/https://ww2.health.wa.gov.au/Articles/A_E/Campaign-COVID-19
column88: On 3 November 2020, the WA Chief Medical Officer reiterated that the existing testing requirements continued to apply, namely that a test should only be requested if a patient has one or more of: a fever of 37.5 degrees or above; or a recent history of fever; or symptoms of acute respiratory infection; or loss of smell or loss of taste. These directions were in force on 1 December and throughout the month of December.     https://web.archive.org/web/20211004023231/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-11/CHO-Approval-Testing-travellers-for-Presentation-Directions-No-7.pdf
column90: A WA Auditor-General report issued on 24 September 2020 outlined the WA Health Department’s contact tracing capacity. The system’s focus is to isolate cases of COVID-19, and quarantine their potential contacts, as quickly as possible. The contact tracing system includes a tracing team of about 50 staff, primarily nurses and other health professionals, and an automated information system. The contact tracing team monitors COVID-19 cases in isolation, and actively traces and monitors their contacts. The Department of Health is authorised to undertake these measures under the Public Health Act 2016 (WA), which was in force on 1 December 2020 and throughout the month.     https://web.archive.org/web/20210831030931/https://audit.wa.gov.au/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Report-5_-Transparency-Report-Current-Status-of-WA-Healths-COVID-19-Response-Preparedness.pdf
column103: As detailed on 16 March 2020 by the WA State Government, it is necessary for an individual travelling on a domestic flight in WA. Everyone in WA must also wear a mask at an airport or when travelling in a vehicle with a person who you know or ought reasonably to know is subject to a quarantine direction. This direction remained in force on 1 December 2020 and throughout the month.     https://web.archive.org/web/20210511024527/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-01/140121-Aircraft-Travel-Face-Mask-Directions%20.pdf    https://web.archive.org/web/20211004131302/https://www.wa.gov.au/government/publications/covid-19-coronavirus-face-masks-frequently-asked-questions
column106: On 1 December 2020 and throughout the month, no vaccinations were yet available in WA. The rollout of the vaccine in WA commenced in late-February 2021, with priority groups offered the first doses.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210909061304/https://www.wa.gov.au/organisation/covid-communications/covid-19-coronavirus-vaccines
column115: At 11:59 on 18 September 2020, pursuant to the Public Health Act 2016 (WA), the Visitors to Residential Aged Care Facilities Directions (No 4) went into effect. This emergency declaration was made to limit the spread of COVID in residential aged care facilities. Close contacts of COVID symptomatic individuals must not travel to facilities or those that have not received an up to date vaccination against influenza (limited exceptions are in place for this last rule). Further, individuals entering to provide a service for a resident may not do so if it is reasonably practicable for the service to be provided in another fashion e.g via telehealth. This declaration was in force on 1 December 2020 and throughout the month.      https://web.archive.org/web/20210308063334/https://www.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-09/Visitors-to-Residential-Aged-Care-Facilities-Directions-No-4.pdf

column90: A WA Auditor-General report issued on 24 September 2020 outlined the WA Health Department’s contact tracing capacity. Schools: The National Cabinet has accepted the advice of the AHPPC that schools should remain open at this time. Specifically, the National Cabinet has agreed that “pre-emptive closures are not proportionate or effective as a public health intervention to prevent community transmission of COVID-19 at this time.”    National Cabinet also noted AHPPC advice that “More than 70 countries around the world have implemented either nationwide or localised school closures, at different times in the evolution of the local COVID-19 epidemic, however it should be noted the majority of these have not been successful in controlling the outbreak. Some of these countries are now considering their position in relation to re-opening schools.”    Boarding schools: The National Cabinet noted that boarding schools are “at high risk of transmission” and encouraged boarding schools and parents to “consider the risks versus the benefits of a student remaining in boarding school”.    Universities and other higher education centres: The National Cabinet accepted the advice that university and higher education “should continue at this time” with risk mitigation measures, including working from home arrangements where effective. As with boarding schools, group student accommodation “presents a higher risk” that warrants consideration of “closing or reducing accommodation densities” if risk mitigation is not possible.     https://web.archive.org/web/20201031205513/https://www.pm.gov.au/media/update-coronavirus-measures    Therefore, schools remain open (although some private schools announced they would be closing voluntarily). column15: Throughout March the Morrison government opposed school closures on the basis of medical advice, but the issue was forced by Victoria bringing forward its school holidays, and other states and territories introducing pupil-free days to prepare for online learning. On 9 April the federal education minister, Dan Tehan, ordered independent schools to reopen. On 12 April, he said the federal government “wants all schools open”. Tehan noted states and territories had “put in place different arrangements”. “But what the nationally consistent approach is, when it comes to parents who have to work and vulnerable children, schools have to be open and have to make sure that they provide a safe learning environment for those children.”    On 16 April the national cabinet declared that education was best delivered in the classroom but states run their education systems based on their own advice, so states are still free to pursue different approaches.    NSW  Term two dates: 27 April–3 July  Position on schools: State schools have remained open but in-person attendance fell to 5% in the first week of April after the NSW government encouraged parents to have their children study at home if they were able. On 21 April the premier, Gladys Berejiklian, announced planned for a phased return to face-to-face learning starting on week three of term two, from 11 May.    Victoria  Term two dates: 14 April–26 June  The first day of term two was a student-free day. Students were still expected to start from Wednesday 15 April.  Position on schools: On 7 April the Victorian government advised that “most students will be educated from home when term two starts to ensure physical distancing helps slow the spread of coronavirus”. Free internet access and laptops will be provided for students who need them.  Onsite learning will only be available for children whose parents cannot work from home and vulnerable students without access to a suitable learning environment.  On 15 April the state’s chief medical officer, Brett Sutton, said on Twitter his advice to the Victorian government “was and continues to be that to slow the spread of coronavirus, schools should undertake remote learning for term two”.    Queensland  Term two dates: 20 April–26 June  Position on schools: On 13 April, the Queensland government announced that for the first five weeks of term two, from 20 April to 22 May, the state would use remote learning or learning from home. The education minister, Grace Grace, said the government would re-evaluate around 15 May.  Children of essential workers can continue to attend in person because schools will remain open.    ACT  Term 2 dates: 28 April–3 July  Position on schools: ACT public schools prepared to move to remote learning in term two, with most public school students expected to undertake their learning from home.  For parents and carers who cannot keep their children at home, due to work or additional needs, the ACT government will provide supervision at a reduced number of public school sites.  On 23 April the education minister, Yvette Berry, said schools would spend the next four weeks preparing to transition back to face-to-face learning.    South Australia  Term two dates: 27 April–3 July  Position on schools: In South Australia, the advice of the chief public health officer is that schools, preschools and early childhood services should remain open. Parents can choose to keep their children at home.    Western Australia  Term 2 dates: 29 April–3 July  Position on schools: From 26 March, families were encouraged to keep children at home, if they could access the online or other resources for their education to continue. School holidays began at the Easter weekend.  On 17 April the government announced a “soft term two opening”. All public schools will be open, with year 11 and 12 students “strongly encouraged to attend” although parents can choose whether or not to send their kids to school.    Northern Territory  Term two dates: Begins 20 April.  Position on schools: Unless a school contacts parents directly with alternative arrangements, children are to physically attend school. Exceptions can be made for parents who have informed the school their child will be learning from home.    Tasmania  Term two dates: 28 April–3 July  Position on schools: Teachers are preparing to continue delivering learning from home, but parents are advised that “if you have to send your children to school, we will continue to provide a safe environment for them and support their learning”    https://web.archive.org/web/20210628221209/https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2020/apr/13/are-schools-open-closed-term-2-australia-coronavirus-easter-holidays

12th July   Clusters in Victoria and Sydney   Australian contacts tell us that it is common knowledge that no one is ever turned away from a test. It is not recommended by the government still that asymptomatic people get tested because in their results, they provide little yield. However as clusters have. broken out in Victoria and now Sydney, many people have been concerned that there is a conflicting message.  On one hand they're saying anyone who has gone into these areas must be tested regardless of symptoms. On the other hand, they have said asymptomatic people don't require a test.  ***H2 definition is”  "Open public testing (e.g “drive through” testing available to asymptomatic people)." This is true, as asymptomatic testing  is "available" just not "recommended".***  There is a transcript from the Deputy Chief Medical Officer from 12th July that confirms asymptomatic testing:  It has always been "available", meeting your criteria, but going one step further, in outbreak areas the medical officer is recommending asymptomatic testing. "The reality, from the Victorian experience that we've seen, is that there have been many, many thousands of tests conducted on asymptomatic individuals for very little yield- but when I say yield very few positives out of the asymptomatic testing that's being conducted down there.  "The asymptomatic test has a role in places where there's local small clusters, so the Casula case is a very good example. column103: Victoria: Since November 23, masks are not mandatory at all times:  - Face covering: mandatory indoors, unless an exemption applies. column115: "In every state, all visitors must have received this year’s flu vaccination unless they have a documented medical contraindication. Visitors cannot enter an aged care facility if they have recently been overseas, been in recent contact with a confirmed case of Covid-19, or feel unwell.    - New South Wales: NSW Health provides guidelines for residential aged care facilities. Residents should have no more than two visitors a day, no large group visits or gatherings, and all visits should be short and take place in the resident’s room, outdoors or a specified area (instead of a communal area).     - Victoria: there are no longer any restrictions on visits to care facilities in Victoria. People of any age can visit residents for as long as desired, as long as the rules set by the facility are followed. Face masks must still be worn.    - Queensland: residents can have up to two visitors at any one time. There is no limit on the number of visits allowed in a day or the length of the visit.    - Tasmania: residents can have up to two visitors at one time. There is no limit on the number of visits in a day or the length of each visit. Residents are allowed to go outside on trips, and hairdressers can be allowed in. Additional visitors are allowed for end of life support, or if needed to reduce distress and confusion given a resident’s medical condition.    - Western Australia: each resident can have one care and support visit a day, with up to two visitors at a time. Only immediate social supports, such as family and close friends, professional help or advocacy services can attend.    - South Australia: up to two people can visit at the same time for care and support. There is no limit to the length of each visit. Workers must wear a mask where physical distancing isn’t possible, and can work at only one site.    - Northern Territory: residents can have up to two visitors at a time. There is no limit on the number of visits in a day or the length of each visit.    - ACT: residents can be visited by up to two people at a time. There is no limit on the number of visits in a day or the length of each visit."    Source: Coded 2T since there are no restrictions in Victoria.    Source: http://web.archive.org/web/20201223001046/https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2020/dec/07/australia-covid-19-lockdown-rules-coronavirus-restrictions-by-state-nsw-victoria-vic-queensland-qld-western-south-australia-wa-sa-nt-act-travel-border-social-distancing-masks

column24: "As of 5pm on Saturday 19 December, residents of the Northern Beaches Council are subject to a lockdown to contain the growing cluster. The lockdown is set to end at 11.59pm on Wednesday 23 December.    Residents will be required to stay at home unless it is for one of four essential reasons – shopping for food or other goods and services, medical care or compassionate needs, exercise and work or education where you cannot work from home.    Venues and gyms will be required to close, however takeaway food business will allowed to trade, and residents will be allowed to travel to collect takeaway locally." column69: "- New South Wales: anyone can enter NSW. The Queensland-NSW border will be open to all travellers from NSW as of Tuesday 1 December 2020. Anyone travelling into NSW who has been to South Australia in the last 14 days must complete a NSW entry declaration form before entering NSW.    - Victoria: a permit system is in place in Victoria for people who have travelled through certain areas designated green, orange or red zones. People travelling from red zones will be denied entry, with some exemptions. The Northern Beaches of NSW are a red zone and from 11.59pm on Sumday 20 December, all of Greater Sydney will be a red zone.    - Queensland: the Queensland border is open to all of New South Wales and Victoria. You will only be required to complete a Queensland Border Declaration Pass if you have been in a hotspot in the last 14 days, or overseas and didn’t fly into Queensland when you arrived in Australia. The NSW Northern Beaches region was declared a hotspot from 1am on 19 December 2020. From 1am 20 December, anyone who has been in NSW from 11 December must complete a border pass declaration.    Tasmania: all travellers from ACT, NSW, NT, QLD, VIC and WA need to register via the Tas e-Travel system at least three days before entering Tasmania but can otherwise freely enter. Anyone travelling from South Australia must quarantine for 14 days in Tasmania (but may be able to do so at home). The intended quarantine location must be registered through the G2G PASS system.    - Western Australia: travellers from ACT, NT, QLD and TAS will not be required to quarantine or present for Day 11 testing. However, they will need to complete the G2G PASS registration and declaration process. From Sunday 20 December, WA will be closed to travellers from NSW.    - South Australia: anyone travelling to SA must complete a cross-border travel registration, with travel open to everyone. SA has declared Greater Sydney a high-transmission zone, requiring people to self-quarantine and get tested on day one, five and 12. People from the Northern beaches area will not be allowed to enter SA from    - Northern Territory: you can enter provided you fill out a border entry form up to 72 hours before arrival and present it upon entry. You will be required to legally declare you have not been in an area the state considers a Covid-19 hotspot in the past 28 days. Penalties of up to $5,000 and up to three years in prison apply for providing misleading information. Arrivals from a hotspot area must go into 14 days supervised quarantine at the traveller’s expense.From 18 December 2020, NSW’s Northern Beaches area was declared a hotspot.    - ACT: anyone can enter the ACT, however, the territory may declare areas as “Covid-affected” requiring 14 days of self-quarantine. From 19 December ACT declared the NSW Northern Beaches a Covid-affected area."    "From 11.59pm on Sunday 20 December, residents in greater Sydney, which includes Central Coast and Blue Mountains area, can only have up to 10 visitors to their home. That rule is set to stay in place until 11:59pm Wednesday 23 December. People living outside the northern beaches are also not permitted to enter the LGA unless the above reasons apply.    Queensland, Victoria, Tasmania and the Northern Territory have implemented travel restrictions barring entry to residents of the northern beaches, while Western Australia is requiring all residents of NSW to quarantine."    Note: Since Sydney is a NSW capital I have upgraded the code to 2G - since now all Australian states have travel restrictions.    Source: http://web.archive.org/web/20201223001046/https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2020/dec/07/australia-covid-19-lockdown-rules-coronavirus-restrictions-by-state-nsw-victoria-vic-queensland-qld-western-south-australia-wa-sa-nt-act-travel-border-social-distancing-masks

column33: "A lockdown in Sydney’s northern beaches area will be extended for at least another week and a half after NSW recorded another five cases of community transmission of COVID-19.    The stay-at-home orders applying to northern beaches residents north of the Narrabeen Bridge will be extended until at least January 9, NSW Premier Gladys Berejiklian announced on Monday.    The lockdown for the southern zone of the northern beaches will be in place until January 2.    (...) On Sunday night, NSW Health issued new alerts for a number of venues in Casula 34km south-west of the Sydney CBD.    The northern beaches lockdown means indoor gatherings are currently banned.    Outdoor get-togethers of up to five on the northern end of the peninsular are permissible and up to 10 on the southern end.    For the rest of Sydney as well as Wollongong, the Central Coast and Blue Mountains, 10-person private gathering restrictions apply."    Source: http://web.archive.org/web/20201231183830/https://thewest.com.au/news/coronavirus/coronavirus-crisis-new-south-wales-records-five-new-cases-of-covid-19-ng-b881756809z
